items.prose: A logistic model gives a firm log-odds of default $z = 0.8$.
items.question: What default probability is that? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put 0.8 through the sigmoid.

byKey.odds: 2.226 are the odds, $e^{0.8}$. Divide by $1 + 2.226$ for the probability.
byKey.z: 0.8 is the log-odds, not a probability.

items.prose: In a default model, the coefficient on volatility (in % points) is 0.30. A firm's default probability is 0.20.
items.question: Volatility rises by 1 point. What is the new default probability, to 3 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the odds, $0.2/0.8$, by $e^{0.3}$, then convert back.

byKey.add: You added 0.30 to the probability. The coefficient changes the log-odds.
byKey.ratio-p: You multiplied the probability by $e^{0.3}$. The factor applies to the odds.

explain.text: The odds go from 0.25 to $0.25 \times 1.350 = 0.337$, so $p$ goes from 0.200 to 0.252. The rise, 0.052, would be larger nearer 0.5.

items.prose: A collateral desk flags trades likely to fail settlement. Checking a flagged trade costs £1,000; a failed trade nobody checked costs £9,000. The model's probabilities are calibrated.
items.question: Above what probability should a trade be flagged?

byKey.ratio: $1{,}000/9{,}000$ divides by the miss cost alone; the denominator is the sum.
byKey.swap: You put the miss cost on top. The threshold is the false-alarm cost over the total.
byKey.half: 0.5 is right only when both errors cost the same.

items.prose: A classifier's threshold is lowered from 0.5 to 0.2.
items.question: What usually happens to recall and precision?

options.why: More positives are caught, but more negatives are flagged too, which drags precision down.
That is what raising the threshold does.

options.text: Neither changes: the model is the same
options.why: The ranking is the same, but the decisions change at each threshold.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what happens to the flagged group when the bar drops.

explain.text: A lower threshold flags more cases: recall can only rise, and the extra flags are mostly negatives. Lesson 11's table showed it.

items.prose: A fraud model flags 40 of 2,000 transactions. 25 transactions were fraud, and 10 of them were among the flagged.
items.question: What is its precision?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the frauds caught by the transactions flagged.

explain.text: Precision 0.25 against a base rate of $25/2{,}000 = 0.0125$ is 20 times better than random. Recall is $10/25 = 0.4$.

items.prose: A credit model's AUC on test firms is 0.21.
items.question: What does that tell you?

options.text: It ranks well but backwards: reversing its scores gives AUC 0.79
It is worse than a coin, so it is useless
options.why: A ranking that is reliably wrong is informative. Reverse it and a random defaulter outranks a random survivor 79% of the time.
AUC is not accuracy; it uses no threshold.

options.text: Its probabilities are too low by 0.29

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what $1 - \text{AUC}$ means.

explain.text: AUC is the chance a positive outranks a negative. At 0.21 the negatives usually outrank the positives. Suspect a flipped label or a sign error in the pipeline.

items.prose: 10% of a book's loans default. A model says 0.1 for every loan.
items.question: What is its Brier score? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Defaulters contribute $(0.1 - 1)^2$ and survivors $(0.1 - 0)^2$.

byKey.zero: A calibrated forecast is not a perfect one. Each defaulter still costs $0.9^2 = 0.81$.
byKey.one: 0.81 is one defaulter's term. Weight it by the 10% that default.

explain.text: The constant forecast is perfectly calibrated and scores $0.1 \times 0.9 = 0.09$, the base rate's own uncertainty. A useful model must beat it.

items.prose: You want to calibrate a gradient-boosted model's scores with isotonic regression.
items.question: Which data should the calibration map be fitted on?

options.text: Scores on loans the model was not fitted on: a held-out set or cross-validation folds

options.why: On loans it was fitted on, the model is overconfident, so the map learns the wrong scale.

options.text: The test loans, so the calibration is as good as possible
options.why: Then the test set is no longer an honest check.
That mixes training scores into the map and spends the test set.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Calibration is fitting. It needs data the model has not seen, and not the test set.

explain.text: Fit the model, score held-out data, learn the map there, then test once. `CalibratedClassifierCV` does the first three with folds.

items.prose: A direction classifier hits 0.55 over 400 test days. 52% of those days were up days.
items.question: What is the $t$ statistic of its edge over the base rate? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract 0.52, then divide by $\sqrt{0.52 \times 0.48/400} = 0.025$.

byKey.coin: You compared with 0.5. The baseline is the 52% of up days.

explain.text: The edge is 3 points with a standard error of 2.5 points: $t = 1.20$. A desk's two-standard-error rule would not trade it.

items.prose: You have 1,000 days of features built from 20-day windows of returns. You want an honest test score for a direction classifier.
items.question: Which evaluation is honest?

options.text: Fit the scaler and model on the first 750 days; score the last 250 once

options.why: Overlapping windows let each fold train on the neighbours of its test days: the future leaks in.

options.text: Standardise all 1,000 days, then fit on the first 750
options.why: The scaler has seen the test days' mean and spread. Fit it inside the training data, as a Pipeline does.

options.text: Try 50 feature sets on the last 250 days and keep the best
options.why: Choosing on the test set turns it into training data; the winner's score is flattering.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the option where nothing from the test days touches the fitting.

explain.text: Only a time-ordered split with every fitted step (scaler, model, threshold) learned on the past gives an honest score. The validation course builds walk-forward versions.
